strengths: The paper presents a useful Algorithms/General contribution: BFS traversal of uniformly sampled spanning trees provides structured order randomization while retaining a standard causal decoder. Combining locality-preserving generation orders with an explicit construction for conditional completion is a coherent and practically relevant idea.

The controlled comparison in Table 2 supports the central generation-quality claim. With the same model configuration, STAR improves FID from 3.57 for random permutations to 2.24, approaching the raster-scan baseline's 2.04 while improving inpainting FID from 3.91 to 2.39. This is a meaningful quality–flexibility trade-off, even without achieving the best generation FID.

Experiments cover four model sizes, from 261M to 1.5B parameters. STAR's generation FID improves from 2.24 to 1.55, and the comparisons with RAR and RandAR contextualize its performance. Table 3 also provides substantial empirical support for the practical efficiency of the proposed BFS rejection criterion on the evaluated masks.

The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful method illustrations, completion pseudocode, attribution of the tokenizer and architectural components, and detailed training hyperparameters in the supplement. The implementation changes appear modest enough to make the method useful for subsequent causal visual-generation research.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate why uniform spanning trees are the appropriate structured randomization mechanism. There are no comparisons with simpler randomized connected-region growth orders, randomized lattice traversals, or alternative root choices. Figures 3–4 motivate locality and position dependence, but cannot establish their causal contribution; distance to the observed prefix also varies with how much context is available. These controls matter because the principal novelty is the ordering strategy.

The inpainting evidence is narrower than the broader image-editing claims. The main comparison is against raster-oriented RAR, which cannot condition each prediction on all observed tokens under the described teacher-forcing procedure. Table 2 includes a useful random-order control, but the inpainting gain is relatively modest, and there is no corresponding comparison with RandAR or a strong bidirectional completion model. Whole-image FID and IS also do not directly establish consistency with the visible context or boundary quality.

The evaluation masks tokens after encoding the complete validation image. With a CNN-based VQ tokenizer, retained tokens can contain information from pixels inside the subsequently masked region. This protocol demonstrates latent-token completion, but does not establish performance when only the genuinely visible pixels are available. A pixel-masked evaluation, together with context-preservation measurements, would strengthen the practical inpainting claim.

The formal traversal argument overstates its guarantees. Equation (3) is sufficient but not necessary for a BFS prefix: observed and masked vertices can share a depth if tie-breaking visits the observed vertices first. Likewise, a DFS completion can enter the masked region after backtracking, so adjacency to the last visited observed vertex is not generally necessary. These issues do not invalidate the proposed construction or its measured acceptance rates, but the claims should be restricted to the specific sufficient constructions being compared. Algorithm 1 also requires a connected masked region to sample its spanning tree, although its listed preconditions only explicitly require the unmasked region to be connected.

Practical scope and reproducibility remain somewhat limited. Evaluation uses one dataset, one resolution, and connected masks tailored to the construction; disconnected observations and masks covering every corner are unsupported. Rejection counts do not establish actual preprocessing or inference overhead, and no timing measurements are supplied. The code-availability footnote contains no usable link. Overall, the demonstrated trade-off supports a slight preference for acceptance, but stronger controls and a more faithful inpainting evaluation are needed to substantiate the broader claims.

strengths: STAR offers a useful and original structured-order strategy: breadth-first traversal of uniformly sampled spanning trees preserves spatially connected prefixes while allowing varied generation orders. It requires only modest changes to a conventional causal Transformer.

The controlled comparison in Table 2 provides convincing evidence that structured ordering improves generation over unrestricted random permutations: FID decreases from 3.57 to 2.24, while inpainting FID improves from 2.57 to 2.39. Generation performance approaches the raster baseline’s 2.04 FID while retaining greater conditioning flexibility.

Experiments span four model sizes, reaching 1.55 FID on ImageNet at 256×256. Table 3 demonstrates practical acceptance rates for the proposed BFS sampling procedure on the evaluated masks. Architecture, training, guidance settings, and mask-generation pseudocode provide useful reproducibility details.
weaknesses: The central editing claim needs stronger comparative evidence. Figure 6 primarily compares against RAR using raster-order teacher forcing, which cannot use all observed tokens when predicting earlier missing positions. Table 2 includes a useful random-order baseline, but the paper omits inpainting comparisons against RandAR or established bidirectional methods. Whole-image FID and IS also do not directly measure agreement with the observed context or boundary consistency. The results establish an advantage over restricted raster conditioning more clearly than a compelling editing trade-off against flexible alternatives.

The scope of supported masks is narrower than the stated assumptions. Algorithm 1 requires a spanning tree of the masked subgraph, so the masked region must be connected, in addition to the explicitly required connected observed region and available corner. Multiple disconnected holes are therefore unsupported by the algorithm as written. Appendix B evaluates only masks where both regions are connected, leaving this limitation untested.

Section 3.3 overstates the traversal argument. Equation (3) is sufficient for a BFS prefix, but not necessary: masked and observed vertices can share a depth if tie-breaking visits all observed vertices first. Likewise, DFS does not generally require the last visited observed vertex to touch the mask; traversal can backtrack to an ancestor before entering a masked subtree. Table 3 consequently supports the particular rejection rules implemented, rather than establishing the claimed general BFS-versus-DFS advantage. The proposed BFS construction remains useful, but its justification needs correction.

The experiments do not isolate why uniform spanning trees are needed. Comparisons with simpler randomized connected-frontier orders, corner versus non-corner roots, and alternative tree distributions would distinguish the effects of locality, center bias, and uniform tree sampling. The entropy plots motivate locality but do not establish that nonadjacent observations provide no meaningful context; distance also varies with the amount of available context.

The practical claims exceed the demonstrated setting. Evaluation uses one dataset, resolution, and tokenizer, with no timing or memory measurements for tree generation, training, or editing. Moreover, inpainting masks tokens after encoding the complete image with a CNN tokenizer; retained tokens can contain information from masked pixels through their receptive fields. This protocol is informative for token completion, but pixel-masked evaluation is needed to substantiate broader image-inpainting claims.

strengths: The paper presents a useful Algorithms/General contribution: BFS traversal of uniformly sampled spanning trees provides structured order diversity while preserving spatial locality and compatibility with a conventional causal Transformer. The combination of generation and flexible completion is relevant to visual autoregressive modeling.

The controlled comparison in Table 2 provides convincing evidence for the core design. STAR improves generation FID from 3.57 for random ordering to 2.24, approaching the raster baseline's 2.04, while improving inpainting FID from the raster baseline's 3.91 to 2.39. Testing spanning-tree orders only at inference does not yield the same generation benefit, supporting the importance of the training strategy.

Results across four model sizes demonstrate competitive generation performance. STAR-XXL achieves FID 1.55 compared with RAR-XXL's 1.48 while retaining flexible completion. Achieving the best generation score is not necessary for this trade-off to be valuable.

Table 3 substantiates the practical choice of BFS for the proposed completion sampler: across the evaluated masks, it requires approximately 1–6 trials and has no observed failures within 100 attempts, substantially outperforming the tested DFS construction.

The presentation includes clear algorithmic pseudocode, substantial training details, and appropriate attribution of the tokenizer, architecture, and tree-sampling method. Overall, the empirical generation–completion trade-off supports a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The inpainting evidence has an important scope limitation: complete images are tokenized before tokens are masked. Because the CNN tokenizer can encode information beyond an individual patch, retained tokens may contain information from the supposedly missing region. This evaluates latent-token completion but does not fully establish performance when missing pixels are unavailable. Evaluation with masking before encoding would strengthen the practical editing claim.

The principal inpainting comparison is against raster-order RAR, which cannot use all observed tokens as context for earlier predictions. Table 2 includes a useful random-order baseline, but its inpainting FID gap is modest, 2.57 versus 2.39. Comparisons with flexible-order methods such as RandAR, alongside measures of contextual consistency and preservation of observed content, would better establish the editing advantage; FID and IS alone do not measure these properties.

Section 3.3 overstates its traversal conditions. Strict depth separation in Eq. (3) is sufficient but not necessary for a BFS prefix, since suitable tie-breaking can place observed nodes before masked nodes at the same depth. Likewise, the boundary condition describes a valid construction rather than an equivalence for arbitrary full trees. These issues do not invalidate Algorithm 1's connected-mask construction, but weaken the theoretical justification of BFS versus DFS.

The method's supported mask family needs clearer qualification. Algorithm 1 samples a spanning tree of the masked region, implicitly requiring that region to be connected, in addition to the explicitly stated connected observed region and available corner. The evaluation enforces connected regions, leaving multiple holes and other common editing configurations untested.

The proposed explanation is not fully isolated experimentally. There are no comparisons with simpler randomized connected-growth orders, alternative root choices for generation, or DFS-trained models. Entropy correlations motivate locality but do not establish that uniform spanning trees or center bias specifically cause the improvements. Results are also limited to ImageNet at 256 × 256, and wall-clock measurements are absent despite claims of unchanged training complexity.

strengths: STAR offers a simple, useful contribution to autoregressive visual generation: BFS traversal of random spanning trees introduces spatial locality while retaining varied generation orders and the standard decoder-only architecture.

The controlled comparison in Table 3 supports the central empirical idea. Under the same training budget, STAR improves generation FID from 3.57 for unrestricted permutation to 2.24, while retaining inpainting capability.

Experiments span four model sizes and demonstrate a competitive generation–inpainting trade-off. STAR-XL achieves generation/inpainting FID of 1.65/2.07, compared with 2.25/2.58 for RandAR-XL and 1.50/3.40 for RAR-XL. Achieving the best generation score is not necessary for this contribution to be valuable.

The manuscript provides substantial implementation details, traversal-efficiency measurements, qualitative examples, and an explicit discussion of some mask restrictions. The representation-learning experiment also suggests a potentially useful extension.
weaknesses: Algorithm 1 can fail to terminate even when its stated assumptions hold. Consider two isolated masked interior vertices of opposite checkerboard parity, sufficiently separated that the remaining grid is connected. Each mask's boundary contains only vertices of the opposite parity to that mask. In any rooted grid spanning tree, all maximum-depth vertices have the same checkerboard parity; therefore, they cannot intersect both boundaries, as line 9 requires. Acceptance probability is zero despite connected observations and available corner roots. This directly undermines the claimed support for multiple disconnected masked regions. Table 4 tests connected masks and consequently does not establish reliability for the stated general case.

The inpainting evaluation provides limited evidence of conditional correctness. Whole-image FID, IS, precision, and recall do not directly measure consistency with observed content, preservation outside the mask, or boundary artifacts. Evaluation uses a custom connected-mask distribution that satisfies the method's restrictions; standard free-form masks and multiple-hole cases would better establish practical applicability. Appendix A's illustrative multi-turn workaround does not quantitatively resolve these limitations.

The ablations establish an advantage over unrestricted permutations but do not isolate the proposed mechanisms. There is no controlled comparison of corner versus central or arbitrary roots, or against simpler randomized connected-region expansion orders. The center-bias quartile analysis changes image subsets rather than the root-selection strategy, so it cannot establish that corner rooting causes the improvement or that uniform spanning trees are necessary.

Several mathematical and algorithmic statements require correction for reproducibility. Equations (2) and (4) maximize expected likelihood rather than the expected log-likelihood normally optimized by token cross-entropy. The claimed equivalence between Equation (5) and maximum-depth boundary attachment is too strong: the latter is a sufficient construction that avoids ties. Algorithm 1's connection-edge expression also omits the maximum-depth restriction described in the prose, and Algorithm A does not reset the mask after a rejected sample.

Generation quality is competitive but consistently below RAR in FID across all four scales, so claims of preserving performance should acknowledge this measurable trade-off. Overall, the empirical contribution is promising, but the unaddressed failure of the central inpainting sampler and incomplete validation of conditional editing support a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: STAR offers a clear, potentially useful algorithmic contribution: BFS traversal of uniform spanning trees provides locality-preserving randomized generation orders while retaining a conventional decoder-only architecture and enabling prefix-conditioned inpainting.

The controlled comparison in Table 3 supports the central empirical premise. At the same training budget, STAR improves generation FID from 3.57 for random permutation to 2.24, while retaining competitive inpainting performance.

Experiments cover four model sizes, and the generation–editing trade-off is promising. STAR-XXL achieves 1.55 FID versus RAR-XXL's 1.48, while STAR-XL improves inpainting FID over both RAR-XL and RandAR-XL in Table 2. Achieving the best generation score is not necessary for this contribution to be valuable.
The manuscript credits relevant methods, supplies substantial training details and compute costs, and explicitly discusses limitations involving disconnected observations and masked corners.
weaknesses: Algorithm 1 can fail to terminate even when its stated assumptions hold. Consider two separated interior single-token holes on opposite checkerboard colors, with the remaining lattice connected and all corners visible. Their respective boundary sets have opposite colors. In any rooted tree on this bipartite lattice, all vertices at maximum depth have the same color, so they cannot intersect both boundary sets as line 9 requires. Consequently, the rejection acceptance probability is zero. This directly undermines the claimed handling of multiple disconnected masked regions; the connected-mask experiments in Table 4 do not test this case, and Supplement A addresses different assumption violations.

The inpainting evidence is narrower than the claimed region-editing flexibility. Evaluation uses one connected, incrementally grown mask with connected visible context. There is no quantitative evaluation of multiple holes, disconnected observations, or the proposed multi-turn workaround. Moreover, whole-image FID, IS, precision, and recall do not directly establish preservation of visible content or boundary coherence. Targeted consistency measurements would strengthen the central editing claim.

The evidence does not isolate why uniform spanning trees and corner roots are necessary. Table 3 establishes an advantage over unrestricted permutations, but lacks simpler connected-frontier order baselines and direct corner-versus-random-root ablations. The center-bias quartile analysis compares different image classes and therefore does not establish the causal benefit of corner initialization.

The likelihood formulation is inaccurate. Equations 2 and 4 maximize an expectation of probability products, whereas standard randomized-order cross-entropy training maximizes the expected log probability. These objectives are generally different, so the stated equivalence to masked-token training needs qualification. This is correctable, but it weakens the mathematical account of the method.

Some conclusions exceed the measurements. STAR has worse generation FID than corresponding RAR models at every reported scale, so 'without sacrificing performance' should be framed as a trade-off. Similarly, Table 3's annealed variant has slightly better inpainting FID than default STAR, contrary to the blanket claim that it cannot outperform the default. The missing reset in Algorithm A's rejected-mask loop also needs correction for reproducibility.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful Algorithms/General contribution: BFS traversal of uniform spanning trees provides a structured family of autoregressive generation orders that preserves spatial locality while enabling prefix-conditioned inpainting. The approach requires minimal architectural changes and offers a meaningful alternative to unrestricted random permutations.

The controlled comparison in Table 3 supports the main empirical premise. Under the same STAR-B computational budget, spanning-tree orders improve generation FID from 3.57 to 2.24 over random permutations and inpainting FID from 2.57 to 2.39. This provides stronger evidence than comparisons across different model families alone.

Results across four model scales demonstrate a competitive generation–editing trade-off. STAR-XXL achieves generation FID 1.55 versus RAR-XXL's 1.48, while STAR-XL improves inpainting FID from RAR-XL's 3.40 to 2.07. Matching the best generation score is not necessary for this additional capability to be valuable.

The paper provides useful implementation details, computational costs, and analyses of traversal efficiency. Table 4 supports BFS over DFS for the tested masks, and the supplementary discussion explicitly acknowledges restrictions on supported observations.
weaknesses: The inpainting evaluation is narrower than the broader flexibility claims. Quantitative experiments use connected masks constructed to leave connected observations and at least one unmasked corner. They do not establish performance on disconnected holes, thin or irregular masks, or masks violating these assumptions. The supplementary multi-turn example is useful, but does not establish that sequential completion preserves conditioning on all originally observed regions.

The main inpainting metrics measure whole-image distributional quality rather than conditional correctness. FID, IS, precision, and recall can benefit from the retained image content without adequately measuring boundary continuity, agreement with observed regions, or plausible completion. Region-sensitive evaluation and a broader qualitative or human assessment would strengthen this central contribution. The DiT comparison also evaluates a particular latent-blending adaptation, so it supports a narrower conclusion than a general limitation of diffusion-based inpainting.

The rejection-sampling construction needs a more precise specification. Equation (5) permits equal depths, for which BFS tie-breaking matters; attaching masked components beyond maximum-depth observed vertices is a sufficient construction, but the claimed equivalence is not established. Algorithm 1's connection step also does not explicitly restrict attachment vertices to the accepted maximum-depth boundary vertices as the prose requires. Acceptance is demonstrated empirically for connected masks, without a general termination argument or a specified fallback for the broader multi-component setting.

The explanations based on center bias and locality remain partly observational. Figure 8 compares class quartiles but does not directly ablate corner, central, and unrestricted root selection; simpler randomized locality-preserving orders are also absent. Consequently, the results support the proposed recipe more strongly than they establish why uniform spanning trees and corner roots are the essential choices. Overall, I lean toward acceptance for the useful empirical trade-off, but these gaps limit confidence in the breadth of the claims.
